## Description {#description}

Students build and evaluate a robot whose learned policy proposes each action and
whose independent governor decides whether to permit it. Students then measure
the resulting motion, and a new observation decides what happens next. The course
is a proposed hardware studio and has not yet been taught. These materials are still in preparation for teaching in the next semester or year, so they will change as the course takes shape.

## Learning outcomes {#outcomes}

By the end of the course, students can:

- Trace the path from sensing to actuation and name the component that proposes, permits, and executes each action.
- Calibrate sensors, measure actuator limits and latency, and set an operating envelope from those measurements.
- Compare a simulation with the real hardware and explain where they disagree.
- Train a learned policy, deploy it on edge hardware, and compare it with a nonlearned baseline.
- Build and test a safety governor, and defend a release decision with evidence from their experiments.

## Reading schedule {#schedule}

In the semester plan, students read one or two Volume IV chapters each week. The
[lab sequence](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/eth-spring-2027/#labs)
pairs each week with work at the robot station.

## Assessment {#assessment}

The ETH Zurich plan uses this split; each offering sets its own.

| Component | Weight |
|:---|:---|
| Labs 1–2: the station and its operating envelope | 15% |
| Labs 3–4: a learned policy on the edge | 25% |
| Lab 5: a stress-tested loop | 10% |
| Lab 6: a safety governor | 25% |
| Capstone: a release decision defended with evidence | 25% |

## Before teaching {#before-teaching}

- **The station is a proposal.** Before students use it, staff must show the
  complete command path working on the assembled hardware, including the
  independent motor cutoff, the operating limits, and restart behavior.
  Connecting a host directly to the arm's motor bus does not by itself give the
  microcontroller authority over each command.
- **Training needs workstation compute.** The course has not fixed a minimum
  training configuration, policy, simulator, or export path. Staff choose these
  and measure memory use and run time on the actual equipment. The introductory
  course's no-GPU assumption does not apply here.
- **A trial run comes first.** Staff run the full student workflow once before
  setting enrollment or buying a class set. The trial must show the policy
  proposing an action, the governor permitting or refusing it, and the arm
  responding within the measured limits. It also sets station capacity,
  supervision, and bench time.

The [hardware feasibility plan](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/blob/dev/labs/vol4/staff/feasibility-plan.md)
contains the detailed staff preparation. It is a planning document and does not
establish that the station has passed qualification.

## Adapting this syllabus {#adapting}

- Each offering sets its own dates, deadlines, and policies on late work, collaboration, and AI tools.
- An offering can change the task, term length, and hardware once staff qualify the resulting station. The system students build must still separate the policy's proposals from the governor's permission.
- The [ETH Zurich spring 2027 syllabus](https://mlsysbook.ai/courses/physical-ai/eth-spring-2027/syllabus.html) gives one complete offering, with its labs and assessment.
